y-m-76-01.title: Checking the calculation that 'raising 20% and then lowering 20% breaks even'
y-m-76-01.topic: Percentages: the base of a price lowered after being raised
y-m-76-01.goal: Know that even the same 20% gives a different amount when the base value changes, and find and fix the line that goes wrong in a price calculation memo.
y-m-76-01.material: A stationery shop owner set the list price of a pencil case with a cost of 10,000원 as 'the cost plus 20%'. During the sale period, the shop gives '20% off the list price'. Taxes, packaging costs, and labor are ignored, and only the selling price and the cost are compared. Below is the calculation memo the owner wrote (line numbers start from 1).
y-m-76-01.thinking.0: Finding the first line in the calculation memo that goes wrong
y-m-76-01.thinking.1: Examining the base with 'what is it a percent of'
y-m-76-01.thinking.2: Finding the limit discount rate yourself
y-m-76-01.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-01.prereq.1: Calculating by changing a percentage (%) to a decimal and multiplying (first-year middle-school level)
y-m-76-01.prereq.2: The meanings of cost, list price, and sale price (the list price is the selling price put up in the shop)
y-m-76-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in the memo that goes wrong.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write in parentheses what the '20%' is 20% of.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.1: Sale price = 12,000 − 2,000 = 10,000원. (It is 20% off, so subtract 2,000원.)
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.2: The sale price equals the cost, so selling at the sale price gives neither profit nor loss.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.line.3: If you raise other goods by 20% and then lower them by 20%, they return to the cost, so we can do sales the same way.
y-m-76-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first to go wrong. The 20% discount is not of the cost but of the list price 12,000원, so it is 2,400원. The sale price is 9,600원, which is 400원 lower than the cost. Lines 3 and 4 took over the value of line 2 as it was and became wrong conclusions.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the most accurate statement of why the sale price becomes lower than the cost?
y-m-76-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write side by side what the 'base value' is in each of the two 20%.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the result of the calculation that assumed the base is the same with the result of the real calculation where the bases differ.
y-m-76-01.s.s2.explain: When raising, it is 20% of 10,000원 (2,000원); when lowering, it is 20% of 12,000원 (2,400원). The bases differ, so the amounts differ.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.prompt: By what percent or less of the list price must the discount be so that it does not go below the cost (10,000원)? Write the calculation and the reason.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.hint.0: First find up to how many 원 you can cut from the list price and still have the cost remain.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.hint.1: Divide to find what percent of the list price that amount is.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that when the discount rate I wrote is applied to the list price of 12,000원, at least 10,000원 remains?
y-m-76-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why it cannot be 20% using the word 'base'?
y-m-76-01.s.s3.model.0: If you cut only 2,000원 from the list price of 12,000원, it is the cost of 10,000원. 2,000 ÷ 12,000 = about 16.7%, so since the base is the list price, you must cut less than 20%.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.model.1: If the discount amount goes over one-sixth of the list price (about 16.7%), it goes below the cost. When raising, the cost was the base, but when lowering, the list price is the base, so you cannot use the same rate.
y-m-76-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation expressed with a fraction instead of a rate

y-m-76-02.title: Can we say a fixed amount or a per-delivery amount is better?
y-m-76-02.topic: Comparing pay methods with linear expressions
y-m-76-02.goal: Check with expressions that which method is more favorable changes with the number of deliveries per day, and make a recommendation with conditions attached.
y-m-76-02.material: A person who does delivery work wants to choose one of two pay methods. Method A: 3,500원 per delivery. Method B: a fixed 30,000원 a day plus 2,000원 per delivery. The number of deliveries per day is an integer from 0 up, with at most 60 a day. Tips, fuel costs, and taxes are ignored.
y-m-76-02.thinking.0: Comparing the sizes of two models by number of deliveries
y-m-76-02.thinking.1: Making several examples that fit a condition
y-m-76-02.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-02.prereq.1: Calculating values with a linear expression (first-year middle-school level)
y-m-76-02.prereq.2: The meaning of an inequality and comparing the sizes of two expressions
y-m-76-02.s.s1.prompt: Without knowing the number of deliveries per day, what can you say by comparing the two methods?
y-m-76-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put in 0, 10, 20, 30 for the number of deliveries and write the pay of the two methods in a table.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find in the table where the side that is ahead changes.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.a: A: the per-delivery amount is bigger, so A always earns more regardless of the number of deliveries
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the per-delivery amount and missed B's fixed amount. When the number is small, the fixed amount is a big share.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.b: The side that is ahead changes with the number of deliveries, and there is a number of deliveries at which the pay is equal
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.c: B: there is a fixed amount, so B always earns more regardless of the number of deliveries
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.c: You looked only at the fixed amount and missed that the difference in the per-delivery amount builds up with the number of deliveries.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.o.d: It can differ with the number of deliveries, but there is no number of deliveries at which the two methods are exactly equal
y-m-76-02.s.s1.r.d: You spoke without checking by calculation whether there is a point where they are equal. Putting in a few numbers of deliveries will show it.
y-m-76-02.s.s1.explain: A is 3,500n and B is 30,000 + 2,000n. The difference of 1,500원 per delivery builds up with the number of deliveries, and at n = 20 both become 70,000원. Below 20 deliveries B is more, and above it A is more.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different numbers n of deliveries per day at which A earns more than B.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.hint.0: Make two expressions, use the same letter for the number of deliveries, and compare which is bigger.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.hint.1: Decide the boundary number first, and then put in a few numbers bigger than it to check.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 60.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of deliveries must be an integer from 0 to 60.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.ok.c2: A's pay is greater than B's.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At this number of deliveries, A's pay is B's or less.
y-m-76-02.s.s2.explain: A is ahead from 21 deliveries. At 20 deliveries both are 70,000원, equal, and below that B is more. Any integer from 21 to 60 is an answer.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.prompt: Which method would you recommend to someone who does 18 to 24 deliveries a day? Write the reason, including the number of deliveries that serves as the standard.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.hint.0: First decide the number of deliveries at which the pay of the two methods is equal, and see which side 18 and 24 deliveries fall on.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put 'If ...' in front of the recommendation sentence.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: 20 deliveries is the standard, so ...
y-m-76-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that at the standard number of deliveries I stated, the two methods give the same amount?
y-m-76-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which side is ahead at 18 deliveries and at 24 deliveries?
y-m-76-02.s.s3.model.0: 20 deliveries is the fork in the road. At 20 deliveries both are 70,000원, from 21 deliveries A is more, and at 19 or fewer B is more. At 18 to 24 deliveries the average is about 21, so A is slightly better, but on a day with 18 deliveries B is safer.
y-m-76-02.s.s3.model.1: If you worry about the number dropping below 20, B is good. Even if you have many days off, 30,000원 is guaranteed. But if you are someone who mostly goes over 20 deliveries, A is better.

y-m-76-03.title: A label saying 'dilute 1:10': how many mL of concentrate is that?
y-m-76-03.topic: Ratios and rates: interpreting dilution notation
y-m-76-03.goal: Know that even the same ratio notation gives different values depending on what is read as a ratio to what, and decide the amount and fix the notation by reflecting the necessary information and measuring conditions.
y-m-76-03.material: There is a germicidal cleaner concentrate in the cleaning supplies storage. The container label says only 'dilute 1:10 before use'. We want to make 1 L (1,000 mL) of diluted solution. The solution is only concentrate mixed with water, and the total volume is taken to be the sum of the two volumes mixed.
y-m-76-03.thinking.1: Revising the judgment each time new information comes in
y-m-76-03.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-03.prereq.1: The meaning of ratio and rate, proportional expressions (first-year middle-school level)
y-m-76-03.prereq.2: The relationship of the volume units L and mL (1 L = 1,000 mL)
y-m-76-03.s.s1.prompt: Can we decide how many mL of concentrate to put in from the label wording alone?
y-m-76-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write at least two ways of reading 1:10.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each way of reading, estimate the amount of concentrate when making 1 L and compare them with each other.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.a: We cannot decide. We need to know what the 1 and the 10 in 1:10 each mean.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.b: We can decide. If it is 1:10, the concentrate is one tenth of the total, so 100 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.b: You read 1:10 as 'concentrate : total'. You did not leave open that it can also be read as 'concentrate : water'.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.c: We can decide. There are 10 of water to 1 of concentrate, so about 91 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.c: Reading it as 'concentrate : water' is possible, but unless the label says so, you settled on just one way.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.o.d: We cannot decide. We need to know the size of the container to determine the amount of concentrate.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.r.d: You named information that is needed, but it has nothing to do with the meaning of the ratio. It is already fixed that we make 1 L.
y-m-76-03.s.s1.explain: If 1:10 is 'concentrate : water', the concentrate is 1000 ÷ 11 ≈ 91 mL, and if it is 'concentrate : total', it is 100 mL, so the values differ. If the label does not say which, we cannot settle on one.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.prompt: Each time new information comes in, revise your judgment about the amount of concentrate.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each step, write in one line what the newly arrived information settled.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the concentrate share of each choice (concentrate ÷ 1,000) and compare it with the standard 9.09%.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.info: The label says only 'dilute 1:10'. Let's estimate the amount of concentrate needed to make 1 L.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.ask: What is fitting as a judgment right now?
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.after: a and b are calculations that pick one way of reading, and c is a judgment that leaves both readings open. At this stage, all can give reasons.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.0.o.c: It could be 91 mL or 100 mL, so we cannot decide yet
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.info: We found small print on the back of the label. 'Add 10 parts water to 1 part concentrate and mix.'
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.ask: Now, what is the amount of concentrate?
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.after: With 1 part concentrate and 10 parts water, the total is 11 parts, so the concentrate is 1000 ÷ 11 ≈ 90.9 mL.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.r.a: This is the value from reading 1:10 as concentrate : total. The back says 10 parts of water are 'added'.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.1.r.b: This is the value for concentrate : water = 1 : 9. It said the water is 10.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.info: On site there is only a measuring cup with marks at 10 mL intervals. If the concentrate is less than 1/11 of the total (about 9.09%), the disinfection is said to be insufficient.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.ask: How much concentrate should we put in?
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.after: 100 mL is 10%, which exceeds the standard and matches a mark. Around 91 mL is accurate but has eyeballing error. Under a condition where it must not fall short, the judgment to round upward is safe.
y-m-76-03.s.s2.st.2.r.a: 90 mL is 9% of the total, which falls short of the standard (about 9.09%).
y-m-76-03.s.s2.reflect: At first there were two values depending on how it was read, then the wording on the back decided how to read it, and in the end the measuring tool and the condition 'it must not fall short' changed the final amount. Let's tell apart whether what the information changed was the 'value' or the 'condition'.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the label wording so there is no misunderstanding. Make it so a worker can read just one line and follow it right away.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.hint.0: Attach a word to say what the '1' and the '10' each are.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.hint.1: Consider whether attaching one example (with numbers) in parentheses makes it clearer.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Reading only this wording, can you calculate how many mL of concentrate it takes to make 1 L?
y-m-76-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you read it yourself to see whether any room for reading it differently remains?
y-m-76-03.s.s3.model.0: Mix 10 parts water with 1 part concentrate. (Example: 100 mL concentrate + 1,000 mL water = 1,100 mL solution)
y-m-76-03.s.s3.model.1: Concentrate : water = 1 : 10. For 1 cup of concentrate, 10 cups of water. To make 1 L, about 91 mL of concentrate and about 909 mL of water.
y-m-76-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that also writes the values

y-m-76-04.title: The screen showed 10.1: pass or fail?
y-m-76-04.topic: Error and tolerance: judging a rounded measurement
y-m-76-04.goal: Work out the range of actual values a rounded measurement points to, and tell apart the cases where pass or fail can be settled and the cases where it cannot.
y-m-76-04.material: The diameter specification of a bolt is '10.00 mm ± 0.08 mm'. If the actual diameter x is at least 9.92 mm and at most 10.08 mm, it passes. The on-site measuring device rounds the actual value to the nearest 0.1 mm and shows it on the screen. Rounding boundaries go up (actual 10.05 → screen 10.1, actual 10.04 → screen 10.0). So if the screen shows 10.0, the actual value is at least 9.95 and less than 10.05.
y-m-76-04.thinking.0: Working out the range of actual values that a displayed value means
y-m-76-04.thinking.1: Telling apart judgments that can be settled and judgments that cannot
y-m-76-04.thinking.2: Making several values that satisfy the condition
y-m-76-04.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-04.prereq.1: Expressing absolute value or a '± range' as an inequality (middle-school level)
y-m-76-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the screen values for which pass or fail can be settled from the screen value alone.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each screen value, first write the interval in which the actual value can lie.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that interval with the pass range 9.92 to 10.08 on a number line.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.a: You read that 9.9 is below the lower limit of the spec, 9.92, so it fails. But the actual value for a screen reading of 9.9 is at least 9.85 and less than 9.95, so some values are at least 9.92.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.b: You did not check whether the whole interval of actual values for a screen reading of 10.0 (at least 9.95 and less than 10.05) lies inside the pass range.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.c: You read that 10.1 is above the upper limit of the spec, 10.08, so it fails. But the actual value for a screen reading of 10.1 is at least 10.05 and less than 10.15, so some values are 10.08 or less.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.r.d: You did not check whether the interval of actual values for a screen reading of 10.2 (at least 10.15 and less than 10.25) overlaps the pass range.
y-m-76-04.s.s1.explain: 10.0 has an actual value of at least 9.95 and less than 10.05, so all pass, and 10.2 has an actual value of at least 10.15 and less than 10.25, so all fail. For 9.9 (9.85 to 9.95) and 10.1 (10.05 to 10.15), part of the interval overlaps the pass range, so it cannot be settled.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the spec's tolerance can be rewritten as ±t mm (pass: 10 − t ≤ x ≤ 10 + t). Make 3 different values of t for which a screen reading of 10.0 is settled as a pass, and for a screen reading of 10.1 pass or fail cannot be settled. (t to two decimal places. A case that passes only at the single boundary point counts as 'settled fail'.)
y-m-76-04.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the two ends of the interval of actual values that screen readings 10.0 and 10.1 each point to with 10 + t.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.hint.1: Change t to 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 and see how the judgments for the two screen readings change.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a positive number to two decimal places.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c1: t must be a number greater than 0 and less than 1, to two decimal places.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.ok.c2: A screen reading of 10.0 is settled as a pass, and at a screen reading of 10.1 there are values that can pass.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c2: If t is 0.05 or less, practically none of the actual values for a screen reading of 10.1 pass (settled fail).
y-m-76-04.s.s2.ok.c3: At a screen reading of 10.1 there are still values that fail.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.fail.c3: If t is 0.15 or more, all the actual values for a screen reading of 10.1 pass, so it is settled.
y-m-76-04.s.s2.explain: For a screen reading of 10.0 to be settled as a pass, the end of the interval, 10.05, must be at most the upper limit 10 + t (t ≥ 0.05), and for only part to pass at a screen reading of 10.1, 10.05 < 10 + t < 10.15 must hold. So any value with 0.05 < t < 0.15 works.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.prompt: How would you handle a bolt whose screen shows 10.1 (spec 10.00 ± 0.08)? Write the way of handling it and the reason.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.hint.0: First write the interval in which the actual value for a screen reading of 10.1 can lie.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.hint.1: Point out which part of that interval falls within the pass range and which part does not.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: A screen reading of 10.1 is ...
y-m-76-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you mention even one advantage or disadvantage (time, cost, risk of defects) of the way of handling I chose?
y-m-76-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you mention directly the interval of actual values that a screen reading of 10.1 points to?
y-m-76-04.s.s3.model.0: A screen reading of 10.1 is a rounded value, so the actual value is at least 10.05 and less than 10.15. It straddles the pass upper limit of 10.08, so we have to measure it again with a more precise measuring device.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.model.1: Since it cannot be settled, there is also a way of treating it as a fail for now and measuring to two decimal places only those that might pass. You can decide depending on which is bigger, the loss of throwing away good parts or the loss of defective parts going out.
y-m-76-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that chooses conservative handling and weighs the cost

y-m-76-05.title: The water bill for a house that used 30 m³: where did it go wrong?
y-m-76-05.goal: In rates where the unit price differs by tier, calculate by correctly separating the part to which each unit price applies, and make several usage amounts that fit a condition.
y-m-76-05.material: An imaginary water rate table. Monthly bill = basic charge 2,000원 + a charge by usage. Up to 20 m³ of usage it is 600원 per 1 m³, and only for the part over 20 m³ it is 900원 per 1 m³. Usage is counted only in whole m³. Below is a memo in which a staff member calculated the bill for a house that used 30 m³ (line numbers start from 1).
y-m-76-05.thinking.0: Finding the line that goes wrong in the solution
y-m-76-05.thinking.1: Checking the change in the bill by estimation
y-m-76-05.thinking.2: Making several usage amounts that satisfy the condition
y-m-76-05.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-05.prereq.1: Calculating a bill with multiplication and addition
y-m-76-05.prereq.2: Finding the value of a linear expression (first-year middle-school level)
y-m-76-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in the memo that goes wrong.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find in which line of the memo the condition 'only for the part over' in the rate table was reflected.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.hint.1: Split 30 m³ into 20 m³ and the part over it, and multiply each by its unit price.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.line.1: 30 m³ is over 20 m³, so multiply all 30 m³ by 900원: 30 × 900 = 27,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the monthly bill for a house that used 30 m³ is 29,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s1.explain: Line 2 goes wrong. The 900원 applies only to the 10 m³ over 20 m³. The correct calculation is 2,000 + 20 × 600 + 10 × 900 = 23,000원. Lines 3 and 4 took over the value of line 2.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.prompt: Without recalculating, what is the most reliable ground for suspecting that 29,000원 is strange?
y-m-76-05.s.s2.hint.0: Apply this memo's method to 20 m³ and 21 m³ respectively.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.hint.1: Work out how much the bill should increase in the real rate table when you use 1 m³ more, and compare.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.a: With the memo's method, 20 m³ is 14,000원 and 21 m³ is 20,900원, so it suddenly jumps
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.b: The basic charge of 2,000원 is too small compared with the usage charge, so it is wrong
y-m-76-05.s.s2.r.b: Comparing the sizes of the basic charge and the usage charge has nothing to do with whether the calculation is right.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.o.c: The unit price was said to be 900원, so multiplying 30 by 900 is no problem and there is no reason to suspect it
y-m-76-05.s.s2.r.c: You multiplied right away without reading which part the unit price applies to in the table.
y-m-76-05.s.s2.explain: Applying the same calculation method to 20 m³ and 21 m³, at the moment the unit price changes from 600원 to 900원 the bill jumps by 6,900원 all at once. This conflicts with a rate table in which only the charge for the extra 1 m³ should increase.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different usage amounts x (m³) for which the monthly bill is at least 25,000원 and less than 30,000원.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.hint.0: First find the bill for a house that used 20 m³.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.hint.1: Using the amount that is added for each 1 m³ above that, estimate the usage amounts corresponding to the two ends of the range.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 100.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Usage must be an integer from 0 to 100.
y-m-76-05.s.s3.explain: The bill up to 20 m³ is 14,000원. Above that, 900원 is added for each 1 m³, so x = 33 is 25,700원 and x = 37 is 29,300원. 32 m³ is 24,800원 and 38 m³ is 30,200원, which are outside the range. Any integer from 33 to 37 is an answer.

y-m-76-06.title: Simple interest of 5% a year or compound interest of 4% a year: which is better if you deposit for a long time?
y-m-76-06.topic: Simple and compound interest: comparing over time
y-m-76-06.goal: Check with calculations by period that the higher interest rate is not always better, and make your own way of advising when the period is not known.
y-m-76-06.material: At a bank counter, we want to explain how to deposit a principal of 1,000,000원 in one of two products. Product P: 5% simple interest a year (each year, interest of 5% of the original principal is added). Product Q: 4% compound interest a year (each year, interest of 4% of the amount at the end of the previous year is added). Taxes, fees, and early cancellation are ignored, interest is calculated once a year, and the period is counted only in whole years. You may use a calculator.
y-m-76-06.thinking.0: Revising a judgment each time evidence grows
y-m-76-06.thinking.1: Finding the period at which the order reverses
y-m-76-06.prereq.0: Assumption: an introductory-level task to try after finishing middle-school math. H1 is only a difficulty label for this batch and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-06.prereq.1: Calculating percentages and powers (1.04 to the n-th power) with a calculator
y-m-76-06.prereq.2: The meaning of simple and compound interest: with simple interest, interest is added only to the original principal, and with compound interest, the interest is also combined into the principal and interest is added the next year
y-m-76-06.s.s1.prompt: Each time information increases by one piece, revise your judgment about 'which product is better'.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write the difference between the two amounts for each period separately and look at the change.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.hint.1: If there is a place where the sign of the difference changes, imagine what happened in the periods in between.

y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is fitting as a judgment right now?
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.after: Both seeing the higher-rate P as better and leaving it open because the period is not known can be given reasons at this stage. Choosing Q on the name 'compound interest' alone is weak in grounds.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: P is better. The rate is higher.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It can differ depending on the period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Q is better. Because it is compound interest.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.info: We calculated the amounts after 3 years. P: 1,150,000원, Q: about 1,124,864원.

y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The two products are the same
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The amounts differ by about 25,000원, so it is hard to say they are the same.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.info: The amounts after 10 years are P: 1,500,000원, Q: about 1,480,244원. The difference at 3 years is about 25,000원, and at 10 years about 20,000원.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the judgment looking at the change in the difference?
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.after: P is still ahead but the difference is shrinking. This trend tells us there is a possibility that the order will change over a longer period.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: P keeps being ahead and the difference between the two amounts is nearly constant
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The difference shrank from 25,000원 to 20,000원. It is not constant.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: P is ahead but the difference is shrinking, so we need to check a longer period
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: From now on, judge that Q is better
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: In the 10-year calculation, P is still ahead. It is too early a ground to change the judgment.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.info: The amounts after 20 years are P: 2,000,000원, Q: about 2,191,123원.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.after: P is ahead at 10 years and Q is ahead at 20 years, so the order changes in between. The side with the higher rate is not always better.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.a: P is always better in every period
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.r.a: At 20 years Q has about 191,000원 more.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.b: P is better if short, and Q is better if long enough
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.o.c: The two products are similar in every period
y-m-76-06.s.s1.st.3.r.c: At 20 years the difference is about 190,000원. It is hard to call that similar.
y-m-76-06.s.s1.reflect: At first both were sensible judgments, but as evidence piled up (P at the 3-year standard, 'still P but the difference shrinks' at 10 years, Q ahead at 20 years), the judgment changed. Say which stage's information was decisive in changing the judgment.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different periods n years at which the maturity amount of Q (4% compound a year) becomes greater than that of P (5% simple a year). (n is an integer up to 30)

y-m-76-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change the period a little at a time until you get close to the period where the leading side changes.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The period must be an integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.ok.c2: Q's maturity amount is greater than P's.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.fail.c2: In this period, Q's maturity amount is P's or less.
y-m-76-06.s.s2.explain: At n = 12, Q is about 1,601,032원 and P is 1,600,000원, so Q is ahead for the first time. At n = 11, Q is about 1,539,454원 and P is 1,550,000원, so P is ahead. Any integer from 12 to 30 is an answer.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.prompt: How would you explain the two products to a customer who does not know the period? Write it including the standard period and what you would ask the customer.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find again, in the steps above, the period at which the two products first reverse.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write one sentence each about which product is better before and after that period.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is there a question asking how long the customer will deposit?
y-m-76-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which product is better before and after the standard period?
y-m-76-06.s.s3.model.0: 12 years is the fork in the road. If you deposit for 12 years or more, compound interest (Q) gives more, and if shorter, simple interest (P) gives more. So first I will ask how many years you plan to deposit.
y-m-76-06.s.s3.model.1: At about 10 years, P has about 20,000원 more, but past 12 years Q is ahead. For a customer who does not know the period, it is good to ask 'Can you leave it for more than 12 years?' and decide that way.

y-m-76-07.title: Is the promotional line 'average delivery 4 days' trustworthy?
y-m-76-07.topic: Mean and median: reading delivery-day data
y-m-76-07.goal: Check that the mean is affected by one extreme value, and choose the representative value and the notice wording that fit the situation.
y-m-76-07.material: An online shop wants to use the promotional line 'average delivery 4 days'. The number of days the 10 most recent orders took to arrive is (in no particular order) 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 18 days. The number of days is a whole number counted from the day of ordering to the day of arrival.
y-m-76-07.thinking.0: Choosing the representative value again to fit the information
y-m-76-07.thinking.1: Making data in which the mean and median differ
y-m-76-07.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-07.prereq.1: The meanings and calculation of mean, median, and mode (middle-school level)
y-m-76-07.prereq.2: Putting data in order of size
y-m-76-07.s.s1.prompt: Each time information increases by one piece, revise your judgment about 'how many days does it usually take if you order from this shop'.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite the data in one line in order of size and find the value in the middle.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate yourself the mean of the 9 orders without the 18 days and compare it with the first mean.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.info: Only the promotional line 'average delivery 4 days' is known. How the 10 data points are spread is not yet known.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is fitting as a judgment right now?
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.after: Both expecting about 4 days from the average of 4 days alone and leaving it open because the spread of the data is not known can be given reasons at this stage.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The average is 4 days, so I expect it generally takes about 4 days
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: If I do not know how the data are spread, it is hard to say how many days it usually takes
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I expect it to take much longer than 4 days
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is no ground to think it takes much longer from the average alone.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.info: The days of all 10 orders have been revealed: 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 18.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the data, what is the most fitting 'usual number of days'?
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.after: Put in order of size, the two middle values are 2 and 3, so the median is 2.5 days, and 9 of the 10 are within 4 days. The average of 4 days was pulled up by the single 18-day order.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You called the one largest value usual. It is only 1 of the 10.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The average is a value pulled up by the single 18. 9 of the 10 are within 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.info: The shop owner told us. 'The one that took 18 days was when transport was blocked by a typhoon, and in the past year that happened only this once.'
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: What number is good to use in the promotional line?
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.after: If exceptions are rare, a number that represents 'most people's experience' is more fitting for notices. Also telling about exceptional delays is an honest way.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Use 'average delivery 4 days' as it is
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The average of 4 days is a value pulled up by the single 18. If that circumstance is rare, it makes customers expect longer than their actual experience.
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Use most people's experience, such as '9 of 10 orders within 4 days'
y-m-76-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Also write the exception, such as 'mostly within 4 days, may be late during typhoons'
y-m-76-07.s.s1.reflect: At first we judged by the average alone, but seeing all the data showed that the average does not represent the usual, and the last information (the rare circumstance) changed which wording is fitting. Let's tell apart which information changed the 'value' and which changed the 'choice of wording'.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.prompt: Set the delivery days of 5 orders from smallest as a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e. Make 2 different data sets whose mean is 4 days and whose median (middle value c) is 2 days or less. (All integers from 1 to 30 days)
y-m-76-07.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what the sum of the five values must be for the mean to be 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about which slot to gather the remaining sum into while keeping the middle value small.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.fail.c1: All values must be integers from 1 to 30.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.ok.c2: They are in order from smallest.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.fail.c2: They are not in the order a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The mean is 4 days (the sum is 20).
y-m-76-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The mean is not 4 days (the sum is not 20).
y-m-76-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The median is 2 days or less.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The median is greater than 2 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s2.explain: If the mean is 4, the sum is 20. To keep the middle value small, the one largest value has to spread far out. For example, 1, 1, 2, 2, 14 has a sum of 20 and a median of 2.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a one-line delivery notice for this shop. Also write the number you would use instead of the average (or along with the average) and the reason.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put the data in order of size and count the orders within 4 days.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence why using that number makes customer expectations more accurate than the average.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can the number I wrote actually be found in the data of the 10 orders above?
y-m-76-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what expectation the wording 'the average is 4 days' gives customers?
y-m-76-07.s.s3.model.0: 9 of 10 orders arrive within 4 days (median 2.5 days). The average of 4 days was raised by the one order that took 18 days, so it is longer than most people's experience.
y-m-76-07.s.s3.model.1: Most arrive in 2 to 3 days and may rarely be late. The average is pulled up by one very late order and does not represent usual deliveries well.

y-m-76-08.title: If 1 of 50 inspected is defective, are there 100 defective in the whole box?
y-m-76-08.topic: Sample survey: speaking about the whole from the sample defect rate
y-m-76-08.goal: The ratio obtained from a sample is only one estimate of the ratio for the whole; work out which whole ratios do not conflict with this result, and say what more needs to be known.
y-m-76-08.material:
One box at a parts factory holds 5,000 parts. An inspector took 50 at random from the box and inspected them, and 1 was defective (sample defect rate 2%). The manager reported, 'This box has 100 defective parts.' The table below shows 'the chance that, assuming the real defect rate of the whole box is this much, 1 or fewer defective come out when 50 are taken at random' (values calculated in advance).
Defect rate 1%: about 91.1%, 2%: about 73.6%, 5%: about 27.9%, 8%: about 8.3%, 12%: about 1.3%.
y-m-76-08.thinking.0: Sorting out what can and cannot be said from the sample result
y-m-76-08.thinking.1: Judging the range of possible whole ratios with a table
y-m-76-08.thinking.2: Saying what more information is needed
y-m-76-08.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-08.prereq.1: Ratios and percentages, multiplying the total number by a ratio
y-m-76-08.prereq.2: The concept that probability is a number between 0 and 1 and shows 'the chance of happening' (middle-school level)
y-m-76-08.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting evaluation of the manager's report of '100 defective'?
y-m-76-08.s.s1.hint.0: Work out how many %p the difference is between getting 1 defective and getting 2 defective when the sample is 50.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.hint.1: Say one reason why the whole defect rate can differ even when the sample defect rate is the same.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.a: The sample is only 1% of the box, so this result gives no clue at all about the whole
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.a: What matters more than what percent of the whole the sample is are the size of the sample and the way it was drawn. It is not that there is no clue at all.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.b: The sample defect rate of 2% is the whole defect rate, so the defective parts are exactly 100
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.b: You took the sample result to be exactly the same as the whole. If a different 50 had been drawn, a different result could have come out.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.c: The whole defect rate could be higher or lower than 2%, and 100 is just one estimate
y-m-76-08.s.s1.o.d: The whole defect rate could be higher than 2%, but there is almost no chance it is lower
y-m-76-08.s.s1.r.d: There is nothing in the sample for the reason you saw almost no chance of it being lower. Getting 1 in the sample can also be explained by chance.
y-m-76-08.s.s1.explain: The 100 obtained by multiplying the sample ratio of 2% is one estimate. At other whole defect rates too, 1 or fewer defective out of 50 can quite easily come out.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.prompt: Let's say that a whole defect rate whose chance in the table is 10% or more 'does not conflict with this sample result'. Choose all the whole defect rates that do not conflict.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.hint.0: On the table, mark the rows where the chance is greater than 10%.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.hint.1: For each defect rate you marked, convert how many defective that is out of 5,000.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.r.d: At 8%, the chance of getting 1 or fewer is about 8.3%, which is less than 10%. You compared the sizes wrongly when reading the standard.
y-m-76-08.s.s2.r.e: At 12%, the chance of getting 1 or fewer is about 1.3%, which is very low. You did not read the values in the table.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the report wording to send to the manager. Put the uncertain points in the sentence, and also write what more must be done to know more precisely.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write the smallest and largest of the non-conflicting defect rates in the table.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write one way to change the inspection to narrow that range.
y-m-76-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The defective parts in this box are ...
y-m-76-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you avoid writing '100' as it is and use a range or the word estimate?
y-m-76-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you guess why increasing the sample would help?
y-m-76-08.s.s3.model.1: We cannot say there are 100 defective. Getting 1 could be chance, so inspect more at random, see whether a similar defect rate comes out, and report it as a range.

y-m-76-09.title: Is a product whose alarm went off 90% likely to be defective?
y-m-76-09.topic: Conditional probability: the relationship between alarm and defect
y-m-76-09.goal: Check with counts that 'if defective, the alarm goes off' and 'the alarm went off, so it is defective' are different statements, and work out for yourself how the value changes when the defect rate changes.
y-m-76-09.material: A factory's inspection machine sounds an alarm with 90% probability if a product is defective, and even for a normal product it sounds an alarm with 5% probability (a false alarm). Apart from this alarm, there is no way to tell whether a product is defective. The defect rate (the share of defective items among all products) can differ from line to line.
y-m-76-09.thinking.0: Revising a probability judgment with new information
y-m-76-09.thinking.1: Finding several defect rates that fit a condition
y-m-76-09.thinking.2: Writing a notice for the work site
y-m-76-09.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-09.prereq.1: The meaning of probability and expressing it as a ratio (middle-school level)
y-m-76-09.s.s1.prompt: Each time information increases by one piece, revise your judgment about 'the chance that a product whose alarm went off is actually defective'.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.hint.0: Split 1,000 items into defective and normal, and write, like a table, the number of each for which the alarm goes off.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.hint.1: Collect only the items whose alarm went off and count how many of them are defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.info: Only the machine's performance (alarm 90% if defective, 5% if normal) is known. We do not know how common defects are.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is a fitting judgment about the probability that a product whose alarm went off is actually defective?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.after: The share of defective items among those whose alarm went off depends on whether defects are very common or very rare, so it cannot be decided from this information alone.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We can say it is about 90%
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the 90% probability of 'alarm if defective' as the probability of 'defective if alarm'.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It cannot be decided unless we know how common defects are
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is about 50%, because it is either defective or not, one of the two
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Having two cases does not mean the probabilities are equal.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.info: On this line, 20 out of 1,000 products (2%) are defective. The alarm goes off for 18, which is 90% of the 20 defective, and for 49, which is 5% of the 980 normal.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the probability that a product whose alarm went off is actually defective?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.after: Of the 67 products whose alarm went off, 18 are defective, so it is about 26.9%. On a line where defects are rare, there are more false alarms than true alarms.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The alarm went off, so about 90%
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The products whose alarm went off number 18 + 49 = 67, and only 18 of them are defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: About 5%, the probability that a normal product gives a false alarm
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 5% is the probability that a normal product gives a false alarm. It differs from the share of defective items among those whose alarm went off.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.info: On another line, 100 out of 1,000 products (10%) are defective. The alarm goes off for 90 of the 100 defective and for 45 of the 900 normal.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does the probability that a product whose alarm went off is actually defective on this line compare with the previous line?
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.after: Of the 135 whose alarm went off, 90 are defective, about 66.7%. Even with the same machine, the more common defects are, the more likely it is that a product whose alarm went off is really defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It stays exactly the same as the previous line, about 27%
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The machine's performance being the same does not mean the result is the same. How common defects are has changed.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It becomes smaller instead, about 10%, the defect rate level
y-m-76-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 10% is only this line's defect rate. You have to count again looking only at the products whose alarm went off.
y-m-76-09.s.s1.reflect: At first there was too little information, so 'cannot be decided' was fitting; once the defect rate was given, we counted and got a value; and when the defect rate changed, the value changed a lot. Let's say why the result differed even though the machine's performance was the same.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different defect rates p% at which the probability that a product whose alarm went off is actually defective is at least 50%. (p is an integer from 1 to 50, and the machine's performance is the same as above)
y-m-76-09.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a defect rate and count, out of 100, the defective and the normal items for which the alarm goes off.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.hint.1: Find the boundary at which the number of alarms on the defective side becomes greater than the number of alarms on the normal side.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 1 to 50.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The defect rate must be a whole-number % from 1 to 50.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The probability that a product whose alarm went off is defective is at least 50%.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The probability that a product whose alarm went off is defective is less than 50%.
y-m-76-09.s.s2.explain: If the defect rate is p%, then out of every 100, among the p defective the alarm goes off for 0.9p, and among the 100 − p normal it goes off for 0.05 × (100 − p). For the defective side to be at least half, 0.9p ≥ 0.05 × (100 − p), which means p ≥ about 5.3. So as an integer, p ≥ 6.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.prompt: Write a one-line notice for the work site on how a worker should respond when the alarm goes off. Also write why an alarm does not mean the product is confirmed defective.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.hint.0: Recall how many of the products whose alarm went off in the steps above were normal.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.hint.1: Write that fact in one sentence, and then write one thing to do next.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even if the alarm goes off ...
y-m-76-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does a worker who reads this wording stop throwing away alarmed products right away?
y-m-76-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about whether the wording should differ between a line with a low defect rate and a line with a high one?
y-m-76-09.s.s3.model.0: Even if the alarm goes off, it is not confirmed defective. It may be a false alarm, so set it aside and inspect it once more.
y-m-76-09.s.s3.model.1: On a line with a low defect rate, there may be more normal products among those whose alarm went off. Do not discard right away; re-inspect.

y-m-76-10.title: When making new item codes, how many letters and how many digits should we use?
y-m-76-10.topic: Counting cases: designing a numbering system
y-m-76-10.goal: Know how the number of codes that can be made is determined when choices follow one after another at each position, and make several designs that satisfy all the conditions on the number needed and the length.
y-m-76-10.material: We are making new item codes for a warehouse. A code has the form of writing 'a uppercase letters' first and then 'd digits' (for example, if a=2 and d=3, a code like KT482). For letters, we use only 24 kinds, leaving out O and I, and for each digit position we use 0 to 9. There are three rules. First, the number of different codes that can be made must be at least the 30,000 items that will be used from now on. Second, so that there are not too many unused codes, it must be at most 600,000. Third, the code length a + d must be at most 5.
y-m-76-10.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a calculation
y-m-76-10.thinking.2: Weighing the advantages and disadvantages of a design
y-m-76-10.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-10.prereq.1: The basic method of counting cases (middle-school level): the number of ways of choosing things in order
y-m-76-10.s.s1.prompt: A staff member calculated the number of codes that can be made with a code system of a=2, d=2 as below. Choose the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.hint.0: Suppose the first letter is fixed, and count how many letters can come in the second letter position.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write out a few codes yourself for a small example (1 letter and 1 digit) and compare with the staff member's method.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.line.0: There are 24 choices for the first letter, and 24 for the second letter too.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.line.1: There are 10 choices for the first digit, and 10 for the second digit too.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.line.2: So the number of different codes is 24 + 24 + 10 + 10 = 68.
y-m-76-10.s.s1.explain: Line 3 goes wrong. Even after choosing one position, the next position can be chosen from all the possibilities, so you must multiply in succession, not add the numbers of choices. 24 × 24 × 10 × 10 = 57,600. The conclusion in line 4 came from this wrong value, so with the correct value it changes.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different pairs (number of letters a, number of digits d) that satisfy all three rules.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one a and one d, calculate the number of codes, and check that it falls within the two ranges (at least 30,000 and at most 600,000).
y-m-76-10.s.s2.hint.1: If it falls outside the range, change a or d by one and check again.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer of at least 0.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.fail.c1: a and d must be integers of at least 0.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The code length is at most 5.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The code length a + d is over 5.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of codes that can be made is at least 30,000.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.ok.c4: The number of codes that can be made is at most 600,000.
y-m-76-10.s.s2.explain: The number of codes is 24^a × 10^d. (2, 2) gives 57,600, (1, 4) gives 240,000, (0, 5) gives 100,000, (2, 3) gives 576,000, (3, 1) gives 138,240, and (4, 0) gives 331,776, so all of these are possible. (1, 3) gives 24,000, which is too few, and (3, 2) gives 1,382,400, which is too many.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.prompt: Pick one of the designs you made and write one advantage and one disadvantage. Use the number of codes (a number) at least once.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number of codes of the design you picked and compare it with the 30,000 needed.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare it from one angle with another design that satisfies the same rules.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the number of codes of the design I chose is within the two ranges of the rules?
y-m-76-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are the advantage and disadvantage from different viewpoints (length, margin, ease of reading)?
y-m-76-10.s.s3.model.0: 2 letters + 2 digits (57,600 codes) has a length of 4, so it is easy to memorize. But if we use 30,000, we use nearly half of the codes, so there is little margin.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.model.1: 1 letter + 4 digits (240,000 codes) is mostly digits, so it is easy to say out loud, but it is far more than the 30,000 needed, so there is a lot of waste, and you have to read a long string of digits.
y-m-76-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that chose a different design

y-m-76-12.title: Sales were high on days when we handed out many flyers: is it thanks to the flyers?
y-m-76-12.topic: Data interpretation: moving together and cause
y-m-76-12.goal: Examine whether two numbers that move together mean cause and effect, and say a comparison method that can rule out other explanations.
y-m-76-12.material:
The owner of a small shop wrote down this week's number of flyers handed out and that day's sales.
Monday: 0 flyers, sales 50만 원
Tuesday: 0, 52만 원
Wednesday: 100, 51만 원
Thursday: 100, 49만 원
Friday: 200, 80만 원
Saturday: 300, 120만 원
Sunday: 300, 118만 원
The owner said, 'The more flyers we handed out on a day, the higher the sales. The flyers raise sales, so let's double the flyers next month.' This shop is in an area known for more customers on weekends, and the owner handed out more flyers to match the weekend.
y-m-76-12.thinking.0: Finding other explanations in the data
y-m-76-12.thinking.1: Choosing a comparison that makes the cause more credible
y-m-76-12.thinking.2: Saying the checks to do before deciding
y-m-76-12.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-12.prereq.1: Reading a table and the tendency of two quantities to grow or shrink together
y-m-76-12.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about concluding from the table alone that 'the flyers raised sales'?
y-m-76-12.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the days of the week on which many flyers were handed out.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.hint.1: Among days of the same kind (Mon to Thu), compare the sales of days with different numbers of flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.a: On all seven days sales were high when flyers were many, so it is fine to say they are the cause
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.a: Having the same tendency and being the cause are different. There may be another reason that moves the two numbers together, such as weekend customers.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.b: It is not enough to conclude. The days with many flyers overlap with busy weekends
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.c: On Mon to Thu there was no relationship between flyers and sales, so we can settle that the flyers have no effect
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.c: On Mon to Thu the number of flyers was only 0 or 100, so we did not compare enough to settle that they have no effect.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.o.d: There are only 7 days of data, so nothing can be said from this table
y-m-76-12.s.s1.r.d: Even with little data, the fact that another explanation, 'weekend customers', can be seen is something you can read from the table.
y-m-76-12.s.s1.explain: The days with many flyers (Fri, Sat, Sun) overlap with the weekend when customers increase. On Mon to Thu, sales are almost the same with 0 flyers and 100 flyers. From this table alone, the effect of the flyers and the weekend effect cannot be told apart.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to check more credibly whether the flyers raise sales.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.hint.0: Think about why the day of the week should be the same when comparing days with flyers and days without.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.hint.1: Mark one by one which choices filter out reasons other than the flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.a: Split weekends and weekdays, and compare the sales of days with flyers and days without among days of the same kind
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.b: Pick only the single day with the highest sales and check how many flyers there were
y-m-76-12.s.s2.r.b: Looking at only the single highest day, you cannot tell it apart from that day's other circumstances. A comparison is needed.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.c: Decide the flyer days by alternating regardless of the day of the week, and compare the sales of days with flyers and days without over several weeks
y-m-76-12.s.s2.o.d: Calculate only the average sales of the days flyers were handed out
y-m-76-12.s.s2.r.d: Without comparing with the days they were not handed out, you cannot tell whether it is the effect of the flyers.
y-m-76-12.s.s2.explain: Comparing days of the same kind, or alternating the flyer days so that the day-of-week effect does not get mixed in, lets you separate out the effect of the flyers better.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.prompt: Write one check the owner should do before deciding to 'double the flyers next month', and the reason.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.hint.0: Check again which days of the week the days with many and few flyers are concentrated on.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.hint.1: Write what days' data are needed more to compare only the same days of the week.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the check I proposed actually separate the weekend effect and the flyer effect?
y-m-76-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about the time or cost the check takes?
y-m-76-12.s.s3.model.0: The days with many flyers are weekends, so there may originally have been many customers. Before deciding, compare days of the same day of the week with flyers and without.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.model.1: First compare sales by changing the number of flyers on weekdays for a few weeks. The current table overlaps with the weekend, so we cannot tell whether it is because of the flyers or the weekend customers.
y-m-76-12.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that checks like an experiment

y-m-76-13.title: How many sandwiches should we prepare: is looking at the average demand enough?
y-m-76-13.topic: Expected value: deciding the amount to prepare
y-m-76-13.goal: Compare the expected profit for each amount prepared from the demand distribution, add another standard such as the worst case, and find several amounts to prepare that fit the conditions.
y-m-76-13.material: A small shop makes and sells sandwiches every morning. Making one costs 2,000원 and it sells for 5,000원. All unsold ones are thrown away. Over the last 20 days, the daily demand (number of customers asking) was 10 on 4 days, 12 on 6 days, 14 on 6 days, and 16 on 4 days. Assume it will keep appearing in the same proportions. The amount prepared is decided as an integer from 10 to 16, and daily profit = number sold × 5,000 − number prepared × 2,000.
y-m-76-13.thinking.0: Weighing the limit of deciding by the average alone
y-m-76-13.thinking.1: Satisfying two standards together: expected profit and worst-case profit
y-m-76-13.thinking.2: Writing a recommendation that takes risk into account
y-m-76-13.prereq.0: Assumption: a task to try after finishing middle-school math. H2 is only a difficulty label meaning one step more careful analysis than H1, and not an assignment to a particular grade.
y-m-76-13.prereq.1: Expected value: multiply each value by its probability and add them all (an extension based on middle-school level)
y-m-76-13.prereq.2: The idea of choosing the smaller of two values, like min(amount prepared, demand)
y-m-76-13.s.s1.prompt: The average demand is 13. What is the most fitting judgment about the way of deciding the amount to prepare?
y-m-76-13.s.s1.hint.0: Set the amount prepared to 13 and 14, and write the profit for each when the demand is 10, 12, 14, 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply by the proportion with which each demand appears and compare the expected profit of the two amounts.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.a: Preparing 13, the same as the average demand, gives the greatest expected profit
y-m-76-13.s.s1.r.a: You assumed that the average demand and the amount with the greatest expected profit are the same. If the loss from leftovers and the profit missed from unsold sales differ in size, it can be different.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.b: The loss from leftovers and the profit missed differ, so the best amount to prepare may differ from the average
y-m-76-13.s.s1.o.c: Preparing 16, the highest demand, is best because we do not miss any customers
y-m-76-13.s.s1.r.c: You looked only at not missing customers and did not weigh the loss of leftovers thrown away.
y-m-76-13.s.s1.explain: When you make one more, if it sells it is a profit of 3,000원, and if it does not sell it is a loss of 2,000원. The two sizes differ, so you cannot claim that the amount with the greatest expected profit equals the average 13. In fact, calculating gives 34,500원 for 13 and 35,000원 for 14.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different amounts q to prepare that satisfy both of the following conditions. (1) The expected profit is at least 34,000원. (2) Even on the day with the least demand (10), the profit is at least 22,000원. (q is an integer from 10 to 16)
y-m-76-13.s.s2.hint.0: Pick an amount to prepare and find the profit when the demand is 10, 12, 14, 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.hint.1: Multiply each profit by the proportion with which it appears and add to get the expected profit, then compare it with the two conditions.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 10 to 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.fail.c1: The amount prepared must be an integer from 10 to 16.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.ok.c2: The expected profit is at least 34,000원.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.fail.c2: The expected profit is less than 34,000원.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.ok.c3: Even on a day when the demand is 10, the profit is at least 22,000원.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.fail.c3: On a day when the demand is 10, the profit is less than 22,000원.
y-m-76-13.s.s2.explain: The expected profit is 34,000원 when q = 12, 34,500원 when 13, and 35,000원 when 14, and the profit on a day with demand 10 is 26,000원, 24,000원, and 22,000원 respectively. q = 11 has an expected profit of 32,000원, so it does not satisfy condition (1), and q = 15 and 16 have worst-day profits of 20,000원 and 18,000원, so they do not satisfy condition (2).
y-m-76-13.s.s3.prompt: Recommend an amount to prepare to this shop. Decide on one number and write expected profit or worst-day profit as the ground, and also write whether the recommendation can differ depending on one's attitude toward risk.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side the expected profit and the profit on the day with the least demand for two candidate amounts.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.hint.1: Find the point where the choice splits depending on how much you want to avoid risk.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you match the expected profit of the amount I chose with the values from the steps above?
y-m-76-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say whether the recommendation differs for people who dislike risk more and for people who dislike it less?
y-m-76-13.s.s3.model.0: I recommend 14. The expected profit is greatest, 35,000원. But on a low-demand day (10) the profit falls to 22,000원, so if you dislike that risk, you can cut it down to 12.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.model.1: I recommend 12. The expected profit is 34,000원, only 1,000원 different from 14, but even on a day with demand 10, 26,000원 remains, so it is safer.
y-m-76-13.s.s3.modelNote.1: A variation that chooses the side that reduces risk
